name: Sissano
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.note: Only wordlists and classificatory works (Laycock 1973/1974/1976, Ross 1988, Churchill 1916); no phonological description of Sissano exists.

new_statements.quote: Stress is predictable in most instances in Arop. When a word consists of three syllables then the stress generally falls on the second syllable except on verb forms. In verb forms the stress always occurs on the first syllable of the verb root. Generally, with word modifiers the stress occurs on the second syllable but always when the word is a modifier with a reduplicated stem. Generally nouns have the stress on the first syllable but will always on the first syllable of reduplicated stems. Although not all words conform to these general rules, stress has a very low functional load and there are some minimal pairs of words elicited where stress is the sole criterion for differentiation. Therefore, stress is phonemic in Arop

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened and rendered pp.18-20 (printed 17-19) to images; also read the tesseract. lines 711-765. Section '6.0 Supra-segmental Items / 6.1 Phonemic status of stress' on printed p.17 (p.18) reads exactly as quoted, word for word ('Stress is predictable in most instances in Arop. When a word consists of three syllables then the stress generally falls on the second syllable except on verb forms. In verb forms the stress always occurs on the first syllable of the verb root. Generally, with word modifiers.. Therefore, stress is phonemic in Arop'); the compilers merely truncated the final clause ', but the use of these words in their gramatical slots negates the nee…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the AROP dialect: stress is largely predictable by word class and shape -- trisyllabic words stress the second syllable; verbs stress the first syllable of the verb root (prefixes get secondary stress); disyllabic modifiers stress the second syllable, disyllabic nouns the first; reduplicated nouns initial, reduplicated modifiers second syllable. A few stress-only minimal pairs exist, so the author calls stress phonemic but of low functional load and leaves it unmarked in orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 6.1.2: in verb forms, secondary stress on the subject pronoun prefix and primary stress on the first syllable of the verb root.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Not all words conform'; listed exceptions include [o.ne] 'this here' (modifier with initial stress) and nouns [a.'mok] 'wild betelnut', [a.'loin] 'feather' with second-syllable stress; some stress-only minimal pairs (not listed in 6.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, elicited citation forms (c. 1,000-word corpus); a stress-marked narrative text is appended (p.30f). Statement is for the Arop dialect (villages Arop), which Whitacre, Laycock 1976 and Ross 1988 treat as one of three ~85%-cognate dialects (Sissano, Arop, Malol) of 'the Sissano language'; Glottolog/ISO now separate Arop-Sissano [aps] arop1242 from Sissano [sso] siss1243. No statement exists for the Sissano-village variety itself in any source I could open.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand stress statements located (Whitacre 1984; SIL OPD 1992 'Sissano [Arop dialect]') describe the AROP dialect, spoken at Arop village, which is now a separate ISO/Glottolog language: Arop-Sissano [aps], glottocode arop1242 (files. At the time (Laycock 1976, Whitacre 1984, Ross 1988) Sissano, Arop and Malol were treated as ~85%-cognate dialects of one 'Sissano language' (old SIL code SSW). Nothing was found for the Sissano-village variety that siss1243 [sso] now denotes; its only phonological description is Laycock 1973 (closed access). To avoid double-counting with arop1242, this quote should not be entered in the catalog under siss1243.

sources.note: Sec. 6.1 'Phonemic status of stress' (printed pp.17-19): stress mostly predictable in Arop -- trisyllables stress 2nd syllable except verbs; verbs stress 1st syllable of root (secondary on pronoun prefix); disyllabic modifiers 2nd syllable; disyllabic nouns 1st syllable; reduplicated nouns 1st, reduplicated modifiers 2nd; a few minimal pairs so 'stress is phonemic in Arop' but low functional load. AROP dialect, not Sissano village.

Condensed from Whitacre 1984; Arop dialect.
